title: The Shrewd Manager and the Rich Man and Lazarus

verses.text: Jesus also said to His disciples, "There was a rich man whose manager was accused of wasting his possessions.
So he called him in to ask, 'What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer.'
The manager said to himself, 'What shall I do, now that my master is taking away my position? I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg.
I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes.'
And he called in each one of his master's debtors. 'How much do you owe my master?' he asked the first.
'A hundred measures of olive oil,' he answered. 'Take your bill,' said the manager, 'sit down quickly, and write fifty.'
Then he asked another, 'And how much do you owe?' 'A hundred measures of wheat,' he replied. 'Take your bill and write eighty,' he told him.
The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly. For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light.
I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings.
Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much.
So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches?
And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?
No servant can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money."
The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all of this and were scoffing at Jesus.
So He said to them, "You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is prized among men is detestable before God.
The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John. Since that time, the gospel of the kingdom of God is being preached, and everyone is forcing his way into it.
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law.
Anyone who divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery, and he who marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
Now there was a rich man dressed in purple and fine linen, who lived each day in joyous splendor.
And a beggar named Lazarus lay at his gate, covered with sores
and longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.
One day the beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. And the rich man also died and was buried.
In Hades, where he was in torment, he looked up and saw Abraham from afar, with Lazarus by his side.
So he cried out, 'Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue. For I am in agony in this fire.'
But Abraham answered, 'Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things. But now he is comforted here, while you are in agony.
And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that even those who wish cannot cross from here to you, nor can anyone cross from there to us.'
'Then I beg you, father,' he said, 'send Lazarus to my father's house,
for I have five brothers. Let him warn them, so that they will not also end up in this place of torment.'
But Abraham replied, 'They have Moses and the Prophets; let your brothers listen to them.'
'No, father Abraham,' he said, 'but if someone is sent to them from the dead, they will repent.'
Then Abraham said to him, 'If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.'"

context.author: Luke, the physician and companion of Paul
context.genre: Parables and sayings about money, told to disciples and then to Pharisees who loved it
context.audience: First the disciples (v.1), then the Pharisees, who are "lovers of money" and scoff at Him (v.14). The rich man and Lazarus is addressed to the Pharisees and is the sharpest warning in the chapter.
context.setting: Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem. A wealthy landowner with a manager who handles his accounts and debts was a familiar figure, and large estates often rented land to tenants who repaid in oil or grain, as the two debtors do here. The rich man's gate and the beggar at it are also everyday sights: Lazarus lies at the doorway where scraps from the table would be thrown out.
context.custom: A manager in this world often added a commission to the debts he recorded. If the manager cut that commission, he gave up his own profit and not the master's money, which would explain the master's praise for his shrewdness. Dogs were unclean scavengers, so their licking Lazarus's sores (v.21) adds to his misery. "Abraham's side" (v.22) was a Jewish image for the place of the blessed dead, like a guest at the banquet reclining next to the host.
context.timelineImmediate: Luke 15 told of the joy of the Father over the lost. Chapter 16 turns to what we do with the things we have been given, and it ends with a story whose rich man, unlike the prodigal's father, shows no mercy at his own gate. The question of whether the dead can rise to warn the living points forward to the resurrection at the end of Luke.
context.timelineBible: The Law and the Prophets (v.16, 29, 31) are the Old Testament Scriptures, which Jesus says already teach care for the poor, as in Deuteronomy 15 and Isaiah 58. His closing line, that someone rising from the dead will not persuade those who reject Moses and the Prophets, looks ahead to His own resurrection and to the unbelief that follows it.
context.sparkNotes: A manager about to be fired cuts his master's debtors a deal so they will welcome him later, and Jesus uses the story to teach disciples to use worldly wealth for eternal purposes. He says faithfulness in small things proves who can be trusted with great ones, and that no one can serve both God and money. The Pharisees sneer, so He tells them of a rich man who ignored Lazarus at his gate. After death their places are reversed, and a great chasm fixed between them can't be crossed. The rich man's request that Lazarus warn his brothers is refused, because they already have Moses and the Prophets.

translation.meaning: An Aramaic word for money or property. The BSB renders it "worldly wealth" in verses 9 and 11 and "money" in verse 13. Jesus treats it as something that can become a rival master.

Wisely, with practical sense. The master praises the manager's prudence, not his dishonesty. Jesus' point is that people of the world are often better at planning for their future than God's people are at planning for eternity.
The realm of the dead. In this story it has places of comfort and torment, and the rich man is conscious, speaks, and remembers. It is a different word from Gehenna, the place of final judgment.
A wide gap or abyss. It is the only time this word appears in the New Testament, and it makes the point that this separation is settled and cannot be crossed by anyone.

gospelParallels.note: "You cannot serve both God and money," in the Sermon on the Mount.
Matthew's saying about the Law and the Prophets until John and the kingdom being taken by force.
Not a stroke of a pen will drop out of the Law, from the Sermon on the Mount.
Jesus' teaching on divorce and remarriage in the Sermon on the Mount.
Mark's version of the teaching on divorce and remarriage.

otBackground.note: God commands open-handed generosity to the poor at one's gate, the duty the rich man ignored.
True worship includes sharing food with the hungry and sheltering the poor.
"Whoever oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker."
A prophetic warning to the comfortable who lie on couches of ivory and feast while others suffer.
The Mosaic law on divorce, behind Jesus' short teaching in verse 18.

commentary.note: On the shrewd manager, Henry says we are only stewards of what God owns, so we should spend it on piety and charity, because "we may make to ourselves friends with it." He warns that "God withholds his grace from covetous worldly people more than we are aware of," since money is called the "unrighteous mammon" and cannot be trusted as true riches. Of the choice between masters he says "their services can never be compounded."

On the rich man and Lazarus, Henry takes the story as a warning about luxury and indifference to the poor: one enjoyed comfort and ended in torment, and the other was comforted. When the rich man asks for a messenger from the dead, Abraham sends him back to the Scriptures. Henry says it is common to think another method would work better than God's own: "Foolish men are apt to think any method of conviction better than that which God has chosen and appointed."

Gill says the master commended the steward not for dishonesty but for shrewdness: "the wit, and not the goodness of the man is commended." He calls riches the "mammon of unrighteousness" because they are so often gotten or used wrongly, and he denies that money can purchase God's favor. On the chasm he says it is "the immutable decree of God" that fixes the states of the blessed and the damned. On the request for someone to rise from the dead, he says repentance is a gift of grace, and that the Jews' unbelief held even after Christ rose.

Lewis does not comment on Luke 16, but his short novel The Great Divorce imagines the chasm of verse 26 as a bus ride from a gray town to the edge of heaven. The visitors are free to stay and change, but most choose to go back, because they will not give up some small attachment such as pride, grievance, or comfort. It is a picture of Abraham's point that those who want to cross cannot, because of what they have become. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)
